summary: Describes a DNS record type that says which host may act as a key exchanger for another host. It is meant to be used only with Secure DNS, so the delegation can be trusted. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a note in the Internet's phone book saying, if you need to swap secret keys with me, talk to this other computer.

subtitle: A DNS record that names which host may negotiate security keys on behalf of another host.

tldr.problem: When one node wants a secure connection with a destination, it must know which systems are authorised to do key exchange for that destination, and it needs a way to trust the answer.
tldr.mechanism: The KX record (type 36) is modeled on the MX record. It lists, with a preference value, the hosts allowed to act as key exchanger for a name, and it is trusted only when signed by Secure DNS.
tldr.outcome: A node looks up the destination's KX records, picks the most preferred exchanger, and runs key management with it. The memo is informational and is not on the standards track.

today: RFC 2230 is an Informational memo, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states it is not on the IETF standards track and specifies no level of standard.

sections.title: Delegating Key Exchange Through DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System already stores addresses and mail exchangers. With the DNS security extensions of RFC 2065, it can also authenticate signed records and store signed public keys. This memo adds the KX record, a way to delegate, in an authenticatable form, authorisation for one node to provide key exchange services for one or more other nodes.

The abstract gives IPsec as an example: a system that wants to protect IP packets to a destination can use KX records to find the set of authorised remote key exchanger systems for that destination. The mechanism can be used with several security services, but only with the Secure DNS.

The RFC says the record was in limited deployment in certain IP-based networks when written. The document is not on the IETF standards track and specifies no level of standard.
sections.eli5: Some computers cannot or should not trade secret codes themselves. The phone book can say, a different computer handles that for me, and the trusted signature proves the note is real.

sections.title: Identity Domination
sections.content:
The examples rely on a concept called identity domination. IPsec has several kinds of identity: IP Address, IP Address Range, Connection ID, Fully-Qualified Domain Name (FQDN), and User with FQDN. A USER FQDN identity dominates a FQDN identity, and an FQDN identity dominates an IP Address identity. A Connection ID dominates an IP Address identity, an IP Address Range dominates each address within it, and an IP Address identity dominates itself.

The memo takes no position on which forms of identity should be used. It only needs the idea so it can say that a security association has, for example, a source identity that dominates one node and a proxy identity that dominates a router.
sections.eli5: Some names cover more than others, like a family name covering every person in the family. A broader name covers the narrower ones inside it.

sections.title: The KX Record
sections.content:
A Key Exchanger record has the mnemonic KX and the type code 36. It is modeled on the MX record, belongs to the Internet (IN) class, and any domain, subdomain or host entry may have one. The textual form is:

<domain-name> IN KX <preference> <domain-name>

Nodes about to start a key exchange with the first name should instead contact the second name. The second name is authorised to provide key exchange services on behalf of the first. If several KX records exist for a name, the preference decides: lower values are preferred. The exchanger name MUST have a CNAME, A or AAAA record.
sections.eli5: Each entry says, to talk keys with this name, call that name instead. If there are several entries, the smaller number is the first choice.

sections.title: KX Record Data Format
sections.content:
The record data has two parts. PREFERENCE is a 16-bit non-negative integer ranking this record among others at the same owner, lower being preferred. EXCHANGER is a domain name for the host that will act as key exchanger for the owner name.

KX records MUST cause type A additional section processing for the exchanger host. If the host processing the DNS transaction supports IPv6, they MUST also cause type AAAA additional section processing. The KX RDATA field MUST NOT be compressed.
sections.eli5: The entry is just a number for ranking and a computer name. The answer also hands over the computer's address so you do not have to ask again.

sections.title: IPsec and Other Examples
sections.content:
The main examples use IPsec. In the subnet-to-subnet case, router R1 decides to protect traffic from host S to host D. It does a secure DNS lookup for D, finds a KX record pointing at router R2, and starts key management with R2. R2 then checks the other direction: it makes an authenticated lookup of KX records for S and confirms that at least one points to R1. If R2 does not get an authenticated response saying R1 is authorised, it will not accept the negotiation on behalf of S.

In the subnet-to-host case, D is its own key exchanger, shown either by a KX record pointing at itself or by an authenticated response saying no KX record exists. In the host-to-subnet or 'roadwarrior' case, D finds that S has a KX record pointing at R1 and negotiates with R1. If the address is known but the name is not, a secure reverse DNS lookup comes first.

The memo also sketches use with a Key Distribution Center such as Kerberos, and with dial-up hosts that get a new address on each connection. For the latter it notes there was no mechanism both IETF-standard and widely deployed for securely updating the reverse binding, and that unauthenticated Dynamic DNS Update is a significant security risk.
sections.eli5: Before two networks build a secret tunnel, each side looks up in the signed phone book who is allowed to speak for the other. If the entry is missing or not signed, they refuse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
KX records MUST always be signed using the DNS Security extensions of RFC 2065. Unsigned KX records MUST be ignored, and so must signed records whose signatures do not validate. Systems that do not implement Secure DNS MUST ignore KX records, because they cannot authenticate them.

A node with no permanent DNS entry that uses Dynamic DNS Update must have those updates fully authenticated, to stop an adversary injecting false KX, A or PTR records. Unsigned false records lead to a denial-of-service attack, while falsely signed ones lead to an active attack.
sections.eli5: The phone book entry only counts if it has a valid signature. Without one, it is thrown away.
